title: Global Systems and Climate Change
seo_title: Year 10 Science: Global Systems and Climate Change Worksheets (Australian Curriculum)
standard_text: Use models of energy flow between the geosphere, biosphere, hydrosphere and atmosphere to explain patterns of global climate change (summary of the Australian Curriculum v9.0 Science content description).
meta_desc: Free Year 10 science worksheets on global systems and climate change: Earth's spheres, energy flow, the greenhouse effect, albedo and feedbacks, evidence of climate change and its effects in Australia. 100 questions with answers.
key_big: More greenhouse gases trap more heat.
key_sub: Human emissions enhance the natural greenhouse effect, warming the atmosphere and oceans.
body_html:
How to think about it

Energy flows between Earth's four spheres: geosphere, biosphere, hydrosphere and atmosphere.

  • Greenhouse gases absorb heat radiated from Earth's surface. Extra CO₂ and methane from human activity enhance this effect.
  • Feedbacks: melting ice lowers albedo (positive feedback) and speeds up warming.
  • Evidence: rising temperatures, sea levels and ocean heat; more coral bleaching and fire-danger days in Australia.
Example

Ice melts and exposes dark ocean. Effect?

albedo falls

more sunlight absorbed

Answer: more warming (positive feedback)

Example

Is a cold week evidence against climate change?

weather is short term

climate is long-term average

Answer: no

Common mistakes

  • Confusing the greenhouse effect with the ozone hole.
  • Thinking weather and climate are the same.
  • Thinking the natural greenhouse effect is bad (it keeps Earth warm enough for life).

faq.a: Mainly the extra greenhouse gases from burning fossil fuels, clearing land and farming, which trap more heat in the atmosphere.

faq.q: What is the evidence that the climate is changing?
faq.a: Thermometer records, rising sea levels, shrinking ice sheets and glaciers, warmer oceans, and changes in when plants flower and animals migrate.

faq.q: How is climate change affecting Australia?
faq.a: Australia has warmed about 1.5 °C since 1910, with more extreme heat, longer fire seasons, coral bleaching on the Great Barrier Reef and rising sea levels.

items.q: Why is warmer ocean water a threat to the Great Barrier Reef?
c: It causes coral bleaching, when corals expel the algae they need.
items.e: Mass bleaching events have become more frequent.

items.q: Less summer sunlight reaches high northern latitudes. Does this tend to warm or cool the climate?
c: it only changes weather for one day
items.e: More energy kept in → warming; less energy in or more reflected → cooling.

items.q: In Kai's model, 340 W/m² of sunlight reaches Earth and 99 W/m² is reflected. How much is absorbed?
What are Milankovitch cycles?
c: slow changes in Earth's orbit and tilt that change how sunlight is spread over the planet
items.e: Ice-age pacemaker.

items.q: Earth reflects 100 W/m² of the 340 W/m² of incoming sunlight. What is Earth's albedo?
A dam is built across a river. Which other Earth system is most directly changed, and how?
c: the atmosphere (cooler temperatures for a year or two)
the hydrosphere and biosphere (a lake forms, fish migration is blocked, sediment is trapped)
items.e: A change in one sphere spreads to others.

items.q: According to the Bureau of Meteorology and CSIRO, how much has Australia warmed since 1910?
items.e: Most of the warming has been since 1950.

items.q: A volcano erupts and puts ash and gases high into the sky. Which other Earth system is most directly changed, and how?
c: the hydrosphere and biosphere (a lake forms, fish migration is blocked, sediment is trapped)
the geosphere and hydrosphere (coasts erode faster without reefs)
the atmosphere and geosphere (more CO₂, more soil erosion)
the atmosphere (cooler temperatures for a year or two)
items.e: A change in one sphere spreads to others.

items.q: How do greenhouse gases warm Earth?
c: They absorb infrared energy given off by Earth and send some back down.
items.e: Outgoing energy trapped.

items.q: What is the difference between weather and climate?
c: Weather is day-to-day conditions; climate is the average pattern over decades.
items.e: A cold day does not disprove climate change.

items.q: Earth's orbit brings more summer sunlight to the far north. Does this tend to warm or cool the climate?
c: it only changes weather for one day
items.e: More energy kept in → warming; less energy in or more reflected → cooling.

items.q: Glaciers melt quickly in a warm period. Which other Earth system is most directly changed, and how?
c: the atmosphere and geosphere (more CO₂, more soil erosion)
items.e: A change in one sphere spreads to others.

items.q: What is albedo?
c: the fraction of sunlight a surface reflects
items.e: Ice has a high albedo; oceans have a low albedo.

items.q: A large forest is cut down. Which other Earth system is most directly changed, and how?
c: the atmosphere and geosphere (more CO₂, more soil erosion)
the atmosphere (cooler temperatures for a year or two)
items.e: A change in one sphere spreads to others.

items.q: Earth absorbs 244 W/m² and gives off 243 W/m² of infrared to space. What happens?
items.e: Compare energy in and out.

items.q: What sets Earth's climate in the long run?
c: the balance between energy coming in from the Sun and energy going out to space
items.e: Energy budget.

items.q: More low, bright clouds form over the oceans. Does this tend to warm or cool the climate?
c: it only changes weather for one day
items.e: More energy kept in → warming; less energy in or more reflected → cooling.

items.q: Ocean currents carry less warm water north. Does this tend to warm or cool the climate?
c: it only changes weather for one day
items.e: More energy kept in → warming; less energy in or more reflected → cooling.

items.q: Earth absorbs 243 W/m² and gives off 243 W/m² of infrared to space. What happens?
items.e: Compare energy in and out.

items.q: Why are sea levels rising?
c: More rain falls on the ocean only.
Warmer water expands and land ice is melting.
items.e: Low-lying Pacific islands and coasts are at risk.

items.q: Which greenhouse gas is mainly released by burning petrol in cars?
items.e: Carbon dioxide from burning; methane from cattle, rice and landfill.

items.q: About what percentage of the air is nitrogen?
items.e: Roughly four-fifths.

items.q: About what percentage of the air is carbon dioxide?
items.e: A very small amount, but important.

items.q: Harper's class wants to reduce greenhouse gases. Which action would help?
items.e: This reduces greenhouse gases or removes CO₂ from the air.

items.q: Mei asks what is mainly causing the rise shown in the graph. What is the best answer?
c: more sunlight from a closer sun
people burning fossil fuels like coal, oil and gas
items.e: Burning fossil fuels releases CO₂ that was stored underground for millions of years.

items.q: Which greenhouse gas is mainly released by cattle digesting grass?
items.e: Carbon dioxide from burning; methane from cattle, rice and landfill.

items.q: Mia's class is studying causes of global warming. How does landfills full of rotting garbage contribute?
c: It adds methane, a greenhouse gas, to the air.
It makes Earth closer to the sun.
It does not affect the air.
It makes a hole in the ozone layer that lets in heat.
items.e: Greenhouse gases trap heat in the atmosphere.

items.q: Which gas is the second most common in the air?
items.e: About 21%.

items.q: Which greenhouse gas is mainly released by rice paddy fields?
items.e: Carbon dioxide from burning; methane from cattle, rice and landfill.

items.q: Ethan's class is studying causes of global warming. How does raising large herds of cattle contribute?
c: It makes a hole in the ozone layer that lets in heat.
It does not affect the air.
It makes Earth closer to the sun.
It adds methane, a greenhouse gas, to the air.
items.e: Greenhouse gases trap heat in the atmosphere.

items.q: About what percentage of the air is oxygen?
items.e: Roughly one-fifth.

items.q: Amelia's class wants to reduce greenhouse gases. Which action would help?
items.e: This reduces greenhouse gases or removes CO₂ from the air.

items.q: Which is a way to reduce greenhouse gas emissions?
c: using renewable energy such as solar and wind
items.e: Australia is a world leader in rooftop solar.

items.q: Priya graphed carbon dioxide (CO₂) measured at Mauna Loa, Hawaii. What trend does it show?
c: CO₂ in the air has been increasing.
CO₂ went up and down randomly.
CO₂ in the air has been decreasing.
items.e: Each later year has a higher value.

items.q: Which greenhouse gas is mainly released by coal-fired power stations?
items.e: Carbon dioxide from burning; methane from cattle, rice and landfill.

items.q: Which sphere includes all the water on Earth, such as oceans, rivers and ice?
items.e: Ice is sometimes called the cryosphere.

items.q: Which greenhouse gas is mainly released by burning forests to clear land?
items.e: Carbon dioxide from burning; methane from cattle, rice and landfill.

items.q: Which gases are the main greenhouse gases?
c: water vapour, carbon dioxide, methane and nitrous oxide
items.e: Oxygen and nitrogen do not absorb infrared radiation.

items.q: Using Amelia's graph, how much did CO₂ increase from 1970 to 2020?
Drought kills plants, so less water evaporates from leaves, so less rain falls, making the drought worse. What kind of feedback is this?
c: a feedback that only affects rocks
items.e: Positive feedback makes the change bigger; negative feedback makes it smaller.

items.q: Fresh snow reflects 85% of sunlight (albedo 85%). What percent does it absorb?
How can cutting a forest change the atmosphere?
c: Fewer trees take in CO₂, and burning or decay releases more CO₂.
It has no effect on air.
items.e: Biosphere → atmosphere.

items.q: Warming thaws permafrost, which releases methane, which causes more warming. What kind of feedback is this?
c: a feedback that only affects rocks
items.e: Positive feedback makes the change bigger; negative feedback makes it smaller.

items.q: A hotter Earth gives off more infrared energy to space, which cools it down. What kind of feedback is this?
c: a feedback that only affects rocks
items.e: Positive feedback makes the change bigger; negative feedback makes it smaller.

items.q: Sunlight of 300 W/m² falls on open ocean (albedo 6%). How much energy is absorbed per square metre?
What are Earth's main systems (spheres)?
c: geosphere, hydrosphere, atmosphere, biosphere and cryosphere
items.e: Interacting systems.

items.q: Sunlight of 200 W/m² falls on forest (albedo 15%). How much energy is absorbed per square metre?
What does a negative feedback do?
c: It reduces the change and helps keep a system stable.
items.e: Stabilising.

items.q: Why does melting snow speed up warming?
c: Darker ground underneath absorbs more sunlight.
items.e: Lower albedo.

items.q: What is the greenhouse effect?
c: The Sun gets hotter each year.
Greenhouse gases absorb heat radiated from Earth's surface and re-emit some back, warming the planet.
The ozone layer has a hole that lets heat in.
items.e: Without it, Earth would be about −18 °C on average.

sets.title: Evidence and effects of climate change

items.q: In William's model, warming is now 1.1 °C above the pre-industrial level and rising 0.2 °C per decade. If this rate continues, about how warm will it be in 40 years?
Why do climate models give a range instead of one exact number?
c: Future emissions and some processes, like clouds, are uncertain.
Scientists disagree on whether CO₂ traps heat.
items.e: Climate models forecast ranges of outcomes under different emissions scenarios.

items.q: Which factor is NOT a main input to a global climate model?
c: the number of cars sold in one city last week
items.e: Climate models forecast ranges of outcomes under different emissions scenarios.

items.q: In Mei's model, warming is now 1 °C above the pre-industrial level and rising 0.2 °C per decade. If this rate continues, about how warm will it be in 40 years?
In a low-emissions scenario, about how much warmer could Earth be by 2100 than before 1850?
items.e: Climate models forecast ranges of outcomes under different emissions scenarios.

items.q: A tide gauge in Ethan's town shows sea level rose 3.5 cm in 10 years. What is the average rate?
items.e: 3.5 cm = 35 mm; 35 ÷ 10 = 3.5 mm per year.

items.q: A tide gauge in Sienna's town shows sea level rose 4.5 cm in 10 years. What is the average rate?
items.e: 4.5 cm = 45 mm; 45 ÷ 10 = 4.5 mm per year.

items.q: Mountain glaciers worldwide are shrinking. Which climate change is this evidence of?
items.e: Many independent kinds of evidence point the same way.

items.q: In Zara's model, warming is now 1.2 °C above the pre-industrial level and rising 0.25 °C per decade. If this rate continues, about how warm will it be in 50 years?
Spring flowers bloom and birds migrate earlier than 50 years ago. Which climate change is this evidence of?
items.e: Many independent kinds of evidence point the same way.

items.q: Which emissions scenario leads to the least warming by 2100?
c: cutting emissions quickly to near zero
items.e: Climate models forecast ranges of outcomes under different emissions scenarios.

items.q: In Chloe's model, warming is now 1.1 °C above the pre-industrial level and rising 0.2 °C per decade. If this rate continues, about how warm will it be in 30 years?
Zara reads that sea level is rising about 6 mm per year. At this rate, how much will it rise in 20 years?
Two models give 2.6 °C and 3.1 °C for the same scenario. What should a forecaster report?
c: a likely range, such as about 2.5 to 3 °C
items.e: Climate models forecast ranges of outcomes under different emissions scenarios.

items.q: In Priya's model, warming is now 1.1 °C above the pre-industrial level and rising 0.4 °C per decade. If this rate continues, about how warm will it be in 40 years?
Which observation is evidence of rising temperatures?
c: Corals turn white and die in hot summers.
Coastal towns flood more often at high tide.
Shells of sea snails grow thinner in more acidic water.
items.e: Match the evidence to the change.

items.q: Why do models run several scenarios?
c: Because only one scenario is possible.
Future warming depends on choices people make about emissions.
items.e: Climate models forecast ranges of outcomes under different emissions scenarios.

items.q: Ethan reads that sea level is rising about 6 mm per year. At this rate, how much will it rise in 50 years?
Which observation is evidence of warmer, earlier springs?
c: Spring flowers bloom and birds migrate earlier than 50 years ago.
Some plants and animals are moving uphill and towards the poles.
Shells of sea snails grow thinner in more acidic water.
items.e: Match the evidence to the change.

items.q: Some plants and animals are moving uphill and towards the poles. Which climate change is this evidence of?
items.e: Many independent kinds of evidence point the same way.

items.q: Ice ages came and went about every 100 000 years for the last million years. Which cause fits this timing best?
c: changes in the shape of Earth's orbit
items.e: Match time scales.

items.q: Which evidence would most strengthen a claim that a region is warming?
c: several independent records (temperature, ice, plant timing) showing the same trend
items.e: Multiple lines of evidence.

items.q: How do trees help to slow climate change?
c: They give out carbon dioxide only.
They take in carbon dioxide for photosynthesis and store the carbon.
items.e: Carbon store.

items.q: What do regional climate models add to global models?
c: more detail about changes in a smaller area, like one state
items.e: Climate models forecast ranges of outcomes under different emissions scenarios.

items.q: Why does a small change in Earth's tilt matter for ice ages?
c: It changes how much summer sunlight reaches high latitudes, so ice can melt or build up.
It changes the length of a day greatly.
items.e: Seasonal energy.

items.q: How can people use climate forecasts?
c: to plan for heat, floods and water supply, such as raising roads or saving water
items.e: Planning.

items.q: Mia puts thermometers in two sealed jars under a lamp. One jar has extra CO₂. After 20 minutes it is 2 °C warmer. What does this model?
c: the greenhouse effect of carbon dioxide
items.e: CO₂ absorbs infrared radiation.

items.q: During the last ice age, sea level was about 120 m lower. Why?
c: Much of the water was locked up in huge ice sheets on land.
items.e: Water stored as ice.

items.q: What is one effect of global warming?
c: Sea levels rise as ice melts and water expands.
items.e: Also more extreme weather.

items.q: Why are renewable energy sources such as wind and solar better for the climate?
c: They do not release carbon dioxide when making electricity.
items.e: Low carbon.

items.q: What does acid rain come from?
c: sulfur dioxide and nitrogen oxides from burning fuels dissolving in rain
items.e: Damages buildings and lakes.

items.q: Noah models sea-level rise by putting ice in a cup of water and on a 'land' block above another cup. Which cup's water level rises?
c: the cup where ice melts from the land block
items.e: Floating ice already displaces its own weight of water.

items.q: What is a limitation of Mia's jar model?
c: A jar is a closed space; the real atmosphere is open and much larger.
items.e: Models simplify real systems.

items.q: Why is a 30-year record better than a 5-year record for finding a climate trend?
c: Short records can be hidden by natural ups and downs.
items.e: Long baselines.

items.q: Why do climate models include greenhouse gases, the Sun, volcanoes and aerosols?
c: Each changes the flow of energy in or out, and models must include them all to match observations.
items.e: Model inputs.

items.q: Ella reads that bushfire weather days in south-east Australia have increased. Which question could she investigate with data?
c: Has the number of high fire-danger days changed since 1950?
items.e: A good question can be answered with data.

items.q: A student says, "The warming rate is the last value in the table." What is the mistake?
c: A rate is the change divided by the time, not one value.
A rate is the first value.
A rate is the sum of the values.
items.e: Change ÷ time.

items.q: Why does melting sea ice speed up warming?
c: Dark water absorbs more sunlight than white ice reflects.
items.e: A feedback.

items.q: Ruby puts a white card and a black card in the sun and measures their temperatures. The black card is hotter. What does this show about albedo?
c: Dark surfaces absorb more sunlight (low albedo).
items.e: This is why melting ice speeds up warming.

items.q: Kai compares ice cores from Antarctica. Layers with more CO₂ also show higher temperatures. What can he say?
c: CO₂ and temperature are strongly linked over long periods.
items.e: Ice cores trap ancient air bubbles.
